description: PWA dashboard for monitoring OpenWrt/GL.iNet home networks: fleet status, per-router health, devices, WireGuard peers, AdGuard Home stats and alerts in real time (SSE). Go backend + React 19 frontend, SQLite, multi-user, i18n ES/EN.

latest_release.name: NetPulse v2.53.0
latest_release.body:
Ten things that were quietly wrong now tell the truth, and the fleet card stops guessing.

- The status of an agent upgrade, a WireGuard transfer and the traffic of a unit all came from the wrong place: a failed agent upgrade left its download behind, the 30 d transfer was a hardcoded fallback, and the traffic chart summed every physical interface instead of the WAN (#2037, #2017, #2048, reported by @edwardally and @fsolak47).
- Graphs and the numbers under them now share the same window, and the 24 h and 7 d views carry four times the points they had (#2046, #2047, @fsolak47).
- SNMPv3 arrives, and a switch no longer reports its CPU interface as a front-panel port (#2042, #2009, @Bann-DEV).
- A unit's health score stops carrying a WireGuard penalty on routers that have no SSH access (#2041, @LemurTech).

### Added

- SNMPv3 (USM) support for polled devices (#2042).
- Per-peer WireGuard counters are persisted, so the 30 d transfer is measured instead of estimated (#2019).
- The 24 h traffic chart draws 96 points instead of 24, and 7 d draws 28 instead of 7 (#2046).
- The unit information card shows the agent version and whether it is behind the embedded one (#2007).
- A guide for contributors who want to translate NetPulse into their language (#2031).

### Changed

- The traffic summary below the graphs follows the range selected in the chart instead of a fixed window (#2047).
- WAN traffic comes from the WAN interfaces only, so the totals stop double counting bridges and VLANs (#2048).
- The integrations page and the README platform table list OPNsense, which the app has offered for a while (#2025, #2028).
- The offline hint of an integration no longer names RouterOS for every vendor, and the raw poll error is shown as it arrives (#2039).

### Fixed

- A failed agent upgrade removes the downloaded binary and its staging file on every exit path (#2037).
- The WireGuard "Transfer 30 d" widget shows the real peer transfer instead of a hardcoded fallback, and only falls back to `wg0` when the listing ran on the router itself (#2017, #2041).
- A single-port access point no longer labels a port as WAN when the board declares none, and a declared WAN survives when the uplink is a bridge member (#2033, #2034).
- A MAC with no lease data stops being labelled as a static reservation while online and as expired once it leaves (#2029).
- A host with virtual interfaces is no longer badged as a switch (#2032).
- The topology map only offers the detail link on nodes that actually navigate (#2049).
- Rack profiles seeded before 2.51.0 show live ports and offer to clean the LAG and virtual ports that stayed behind (#2010).
- A scheduled config backup served by an agent logs as scheduled, like the ones the server runs (#2011).

## Thanks

- **@fsolak47** for #2046, #2047, #2048 and #2049: four reports that turned into more graph resolution, range-aligned numbers, WAN counters and a topology link that does nothing. The traffic screens were one person looking carefully.
- **@crowedavid** for #2007 and #2011, the agent version in the unit card and the inconsistent journal entry, and for the port captures behind the two agent fixes in this release.
- **@Bann-DEV** for #2009 and #2010, which put the switch CPU interface back where it belongs and made old rack profiles usable again.
- **@edwardally** for #2017, the WireGuard widget that had been showing the same number for months.
- **@LemurTech** for #2041, a health score penalised forever by an interface that did not exist.

**Full changelog**: https://github.com/gnacho/netpulse/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md

detail.readme:
# NetPulse

English | Español

The pulse of your home network. Real time. No cloud.
Watch your routers, draw your topology, score your network's health and get alerted, from a single self-hosted binary. Nothing ever leaves your LAN.

Try the live demo · Full feature tour

## See it before you install it You don't need a single router to see NetPulse working: - **[demo.netpulse.cloudless.club](https://demo.netpulse.cloudless.club)** is the real app with a full sample network loaded, read-only, no sign-up. Click around, change the theme, switch languages, watch the live updates. - **[netpulse.cloudless.club/features](https://netpulse.cloudless.club/features)** is the complete feature inventory: every screen and feature, with the technical decisions and the honest scope of each one. ## What you get **Fleet overview and a health score that means something.** One 0-100 score condenses latency, loss, uptime and temperature per router and for the whole network, updated live every 5 seconds over SSE. Live WAN traffic against your contracted plan, alert feed, AdGuard Home stats and WireGuard peers on the same screen (that's the screenshot above). **A topology map that draws itself.** Inferred live from the bridge FDB (and LLDP where available, including LLDP-MIB on SNMP-managed switches): wired and wireless clients under the router and port they actually talk through, managed and inferred switches, Proxmox hosts with their VMs nested, and WireGuard tunnels drawn from peer to Internet. Quiet devices keep their place; nothing jumps around on refresh. Drag nodes to arrange it and the layout stays yours.

**Every device, classified.** Hostnames, IPs, type detection (hostname patterns + OUI), first seen, band and signal for Wi-Fi clients, and the router each one is attached to. A static host that nothing else names, typically a switch or a server that never takes a DHCP lease, still gets its name from a forward-confirmed reverse lookup, done in the background and only for private addresses. Label devices, reserve IPs, and see when something new shows up.

**Per-router health at a glance.** Model, firmware, CPU, memory, temperature, uptime and live traffic for each router, with port-level history and per-band client splits. SNMP-polled managed switches are first-class citizens too, and any unit can be paused without removing it: no polling, no alerts, history kept.

**WAN speed tests, on demand or on a schedule.** Run a test from the server whenever you need one, or schedule it by interval, weekly, monthly, or during the quietest hour based on the previous seven days of traffic. Results stay in SQLite with a seven-day chart and recent history. Choose M-Lab NDT (the default), Ookla, Cloudflare, LibreSpeed or a custom HTTP endpoint, and get an alert when download speed falls below your chosen percentage of the contracted plan. **What it runs on.** The server is one static Go binary on any Linux box. The agent is what talks to your routers, and how it gets there depends on the platform: | Platform | How the agent runs | Notes | |---|---|---| | OpenWrt (incl. GL.iNet) | Native `netpulse-agent` package (`.ipk`/`.apk`) | procd, UCI config, `luci-app-netpulse`, in-app install and upgrade | | MikroTik (RouterOS) | External `routeros-pusher` in [netpulse-integrations](https://github.com/gnacho/netpulse-integrations/tree/main/routeros) | Read-only over the binary API (REST fallback): system, ports, DHCP, ARP, FDB, temperature, firmware and WAN traffic. Deployed and managed from the Integrations section | | Asuswrt / Asuswrt-Merlin | External `asuswrt-pusher` in [netpulse-integrations](https://github.com/gnacho/netpulse-integrations/tree/main/asuswrt) | Static binary under `/jffs/netpulse` (Merlin layout), using `/proc`, `iw` and `lldpd`. Deployed over SSH from the Integrations section, key or password sign-in | | OPNsense (firewall) | External `opnsense-pusher` in [netpulse-integrations](https://github.com/gnacho/netpulse-integrations/tree/main/opnsense) | Read-only API key with minimum privileges: system, interface counters, IPv4 ARP, WAN rates with an explicitly selected interface, memory and temperature. Beta | | UniFi (self-hosted controller) | External `unifi-pusher` in [netpulse-integrations](https://github.com/gnacho/netpulse-integrations/tree/main/unifi) | Read-only, one site: gateways, switches and APs with ports and uplinks, clients with band and signal, gateway uptime. Deployed from the Integrations section | | External router families | Separate Go pusher in [netpulse-integrations](https://github.com/gnacho/netpulse-integrations) | See the [external integrations guide](docs/external-integrations.md) | | Managed switches | SNMP | Port states, speeds and LLDP-MIB neighbours | | Realtek switches (RTL8372/8373) | Embedded beacon in the [RTLPlayground fork](https://github.com/gnacho/RTLPlayground) | Port state, byte rates and FDB over UDP. Advanced firmware setup, see the [Realtek switch beacon guide](docs/RTL-SWITCH-BEACON.md) | Vendor integrations live outside the server on purpose. An OpenWrt router never carries code for RouterOS, Bbox or another platform, and each integration can be tested and released on its own schedule. Whoever owns the hardware validates it, while NetPulse maintains only the shared ingest contract. **And the rest of the tour:** - **WireGuard**: peers with real names, latest handshakes, transfer per peer and the traffic of the last 30 days, built from persisted per-peer counters because the counters WireGuard exposes restart at zero with every peer. - **AdGuard Home**: query stats, blocked share, top blocked domains. - **Wi-Fi and roaming**: signal matrix per AP, 802.11r status, channel utilization, persistent roaming events. - **Wi-Fi channel analyzer**: a real spectrum per radio, every network drawn on the frequency axis with a congestion score for every channel. It reads the air and advises; it never writes to your routers. - **Fleet firmware upgrades**: upgrade OpenWrt devices from the UI, vanilla OpenWrt only (device list filtered, with an explanatory note). - **Physical rack (Labs preview)**: draw your 19" rack, place your hardware and let NetPulse propose the cabling from the detected topology. Off by default. - **Alerts that find you**: temperature, new device, firmware available, WAN down, agent issues; bell feed plus notification channels (native Web Push, ntfy, Telegram and outgoing webhook). Notification channels only carry alerts marked as urgent; the feed level (none / urgent / all) is configured separately in Alerts. - **Multi-user**: bcrypt passwords, admin and viewer roles, per-user language (ES/EN). - **Installable PWA**: phone or desktop, live over SSE, light/dark themes. - **A good OpenWrt citizen**: native `netpulse-agent` packages (`.ipk`/`.apk`), a `luci-app-netpulse` page, UCI config, procd init with self-heal. Or run the whole server on-box. - **Self-updating**: the built-in updater checks for releases and applies them with an atomic swap. - **MQTT + Home Assistant (opt-in)**: publish the fleet state (health, clients, per-router vitals and alerts) to an MQTT broker; Home Assistant discovers the entities on its own. Routers that expose themselves with NetGrip are not duplicated. Off by default and cloud-free: configured from the MQTT card in Settings (or with the `NETPULSE_MQTT_*` environment variables, or the equivalent `mqtt_*` UCI options on-box). Topics, entities and limits in the [manual](docs/manual.en.md#home-assistant-mqtt). **An MCP server for your AI assistant.** NetPulse embeds a read-only [MCP](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) server (streamable HTTP at `/mcp`) so your assistant can query fleet status, per-router health, known devices, WireGuard peers, AdGuard Home stats, the topology graph and active alerts with an API token. Token-only auth (never the session cookie), rate limited, every call logged for audit. Disabled by default: enable it with `NETPULSE_MCP_ENABLED=1` and mint a token in Settings → API tokens. Keep the port on your LAN: anyone with the token can read your whole network state. That is still a selection: **[every feature is on the website](https://netpulse.cloudless.club/features)**, one by one, and everything above is clickable in the **[live demo](https://demo.netpulse.cloudless.club)**. ## Get started in about five minutes You need a Linux box with systemd (x86_64, arm64 or armv7; a small LXC or VM is plenty) and OpenWrt/GL.iNet routers on your LAN. MikroTik, Asuswrt/Merlin, OPNsense and UniFi controllers are supported through app-managed integrations, and anything with SSH or SNMP can be added by hand (see the folded section below). **1. Install the server** on the box: ```bash curl -fsSL --retry 3 -o /tmp/netpulse-install.sh https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gnacho/netpulse/main/install.sh && sh /tmp/netpulse-install.sh ``` The installer is plain, readable shell ([inspect it first](install.sh)): it detects distro and arch, downloads the release verified against `checksums.txt`, sets up a sandboxed `netpulse` systemd service and prints the initial admin password once. Re-running the same line updates; `sh install.sh --uninstall` removes. **2. Open the app** at `http://:3000`, log in with the printed password and the gateway is already there: NetPulse finds it on first boot via LAN discovery (a TCP :22 sweep with ubus/GL-UI fingerprinting). **3. Authorize the SSH key.** The server generated its own keypair on first boot. Copy the public key from **Settings → Fleet** and, on each router you want to monitor, append it: ```sh echo "" >> /etc/dropbear/authorized_keys ``` **4. Install the agents from the app.** Open **Routers** and scroll to the agents table: every OpenWrt router gets a row, and routers without an agent offer an **Install agent** button. One click and the server registers the agent, pushes the right binary for the router's architecture, writes the config and starts the service; it shows up as connected within seconds. Routers the server cannot SSH into use the pairing token instead (**Settings → Agent adoption**, see the folded section below). Asuswrt/Merlin, MikroTik, OPNsense and UniFi controllers use the vendor pushers from the Integrations section instead. **5. Take it with you.** Install the PWA from your browser (Add to home screen / Install app) and enable Web Push in Settings: alerts reach your phone even with the tab closed. Prefer to see it on your own hardware first? `DEMO_MODE=1 AUTH_PASS=choose-one ./netpulse` runs the same app with a 67-device sample network, no routers needed. `AUTH_PASS` is required even in demo mode: it protects the web session.
Other install paths **OpenWrt packages.** Every release ships `netpulse-agent` and `luci-app-netpulse` as installable packages (`.ipk` for OpenWrt 24.10, `.apk` for 25.12, plus x86/64). Grab them from the [latest release](https://github.com/gnacho/netpulse/releases): ```sh # OpenWrt 24.10 (ipk) opkg install ./netpulse-agent_*.ipk ./luci-app-netpulse_*.ipk # OpenWrt 25.12 (apk) apk add --allow-untrusted ./netpulse-agent-*.apk ./luci-app-netpulse-*.apk ``` The package ships an empty config, so point it at your server before starting: ```sh uci set netpulse-agent.main.server='http://:3000' uci set netpulse-agent.main.slug='' uci set netpulse-agent.main.token='<64-hex token>' uci commit netpulse-agent service netpulse-agent enable && service netpulse-agent start ``` If the server can already SSH into the router, skip all of this and press **Install agent** in the app: it does every step for you. **Pairing token.** For routers the server cannot reach over SSH, Settings → Agent adoption shows a reusable pairing token: `install-agent.sh --pairing-token` (run from any machine that can reach both the router and the server) registers the agent on first contact. **Asuswrt / Merlin.** Support lives in the external [`asuswrt-pusher`](https://github.com/gnacho/netpulse-integrations/tree/main/asuswrt) integration. Build its static binary, create the router as type `external` and copy the binary and environment file to `/jffs/`, which survives firmware updates. The integration README covers boot startup and manual upgrades. The pusher uses the portable probes for system data, wireless, DHCP, bridge FDB, ARP and LLDP. Features that require `ubus` or GL.iNet services remain absent, and the native agent upgrade and reinstall actions are not available. From the Integrations section the app can also install the pusher for you over SSH. An authorized server key is still the preferred path; when the router only accepts passwords, like the dropbear of a stock Asuswrt, set the password in the form and the server signs in with it. The password is stored in a 0600 companion file next to the integration environment file, never in the database, and a wrong password reports `ssh_auth_failed` instead of a generic SSH failure. **Latency sidecar.** Optional long-term TCP latency probes per router: ```bash curl -fsSL --retry 3 -o /tmp/netpulse-install-collector.sh https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gnacho/netpulse/main/install-collector.sh && sh /tmp/netpulse-install-collector.sh ``` Each probe is a TCP connection to the router that is closed without authenticating, so a router with dropbear logs it as `Child connection` followed by `Exit before auth: Exited normally`. That is the probe, not a failed login. `PROBE_PORT` (default `22`) points it at a listener that does not log every connection, for example the router's web UI on `80`, and `PROBE_INTERVAL` (default `5s`) sets how often it runs. **On-box mode.** No spare box? The server itself runs on an OpenWrt router, with UCI config and self-signed TLS with SPKI pinning.
## Updates and version history Releases are signed, checksummed and pushed to your fleet by the built-in auto-updater; the app shows a short human-readable "what changed" panel before you update. The full version history lives in [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md) and on the [releases page](https://github.com/gnacho/netpulse/releases); the plan ahead is in [docs/ROADMAP.md](docs/ROADMAP.md). ## Documentation - **[User manual](docs/manual.en.md)** (also in [Spanish](docs/manual.es.md)): every screen explained, menu by menu, with step-by-step procedures. - **[Website](https://netpulse.cloudless.club)**: the project in five minutes, with a [feature tour](https://netpulse.cloudless.club/features), FAQ and screenshots. - **[Translations](docs/translations.md)**: how to add a language to the landing or to the panel, and what we check before merging it. - **[Roadmap](docs/ROADMAP.md)**: what's done, what's next. - **[Discussions](https://github.com/gnacho/netpulse/discussions)**: questions, ideas and shape-the-future talk. ## Big thanks NetPulse wouldn't exist without [OpenWrt](https://openwrt.org/). The whole premise of the project, that you can own and control your network hardware instead of depending on a vendor's closed firmware, only works because OpenWrt exists. If NetPulse is useful to you, the real credit goes to the OpenWrt community. This project is also shaped by its community: every issue, pull request and real-hardware test makes it better. Thanks to everyone who has contributed so far - the people and the work behind each release are named in the [CHANGELOG](CHANGELOG.md) and in every release's notes. If you want to send code, read [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) first: every PR runs the full build and test suite, and new server code lives in its own file with its test. ## Star history [![Star History Chart](https://api.star-history.com/svg?repos=gnacho/netpulse&type=date)](https://www.star-history.com/#gnacho/netpulse&date) ## License [AGPL-3.0](LICENSE)
